query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy featuring a lamellar microstructure composed of alternating softer fcc and harder B2 phases, exposure at elevated temperature (≈700 °C) under simultaneous wear and a corrosive environment (chloride-containing sulfuric acid solution) results in accelerated degradation due to wear-induced spallation of a nascent, protective oxide film on the softer fcc phase. The mechanical removal of this film at phase boundaries locally exposes anodic regions, which, via galvanic coupling with the relatively nobler B2 phase, enhances localized corrosion, thereby coupling with abrasive wear to increase total degradation relative to conditions where wear or corrosion acts alone.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA with a uniform, fine lamellar microstructure (≈2 μm interlamellar spacing) featuring alternating fcc (softer, Al- and Ni-rich) and B2 (harder, Co-, Cr-, Fe-rich) phases as characterized in PMC4145285::web::004::microstructure_and_phase_constitution.
generation.intervention: Apply simultaneous mechanical sliding wear (using a standardized ball-on-disk apparatus with controlled normal load and sliding speed) in a corrosive environment, namely a chloride-containing sulfuric acid solution, at 700 °C. For controlled comparison, prepare a matched baseline sample where either the wear or the corrosion condition is isolated, and a microstructurally modified variant with refined lamellar spacing to reduce phase boundary area.
generation.conditions: Temperature at approximately 700 °C; corrosive environment defined as a chloride-containing sulfuric acid solution (composition as per ASTM standards); fixed contact load and sliding speed replicating service conditions; tests performed for a duration sufficient to establish steady-state degradation (e.g. 100 hours).
generation.structural_mediator: The lamellar phase boundaries between the softer fcc and harder B2 phases serve as mediators where differences in oxidation behavior and mechanical wear response coexist. These boundaries foster localized galvanic cells once the protective oxide is locally removed by mechanical wear.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, a protective oxide (likely Al2O3 or spinel phases) initially forms on both phases; however, due to the softer fcc phase, the oxide is more susceptible to mechanical wear, leading to its spallation particularly at the fcc/B2 interfaces. The exposed anodic fcc regions are then preferentially corroded via galvanic action against the relatively inert B2 regions, resulting in accelerated degradation through the synergistic interaction of wear and corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline tests (individual wear or corrosion), the simultaneous application of wear and corrosion will result in a significant increase in total material degradation (e.g., an expected increase in the degradation rate by a rough order of magnitude, subject to verification), with distinct local features: increased depth and density of corrosion pits at phase boundaries, higher wear track damage, and reduced protective oxide layer continuity. The microstructurally modified variant with refined lamellar spacing is predicted to show a reduction (approximately 30% lower) in overall degradation, along with less pronounced localized galvanic attack.
generation.baseline: Comparative tests on the same alloy under isolated conditions: (i) wear in a non-corrosive inert environment, (ii) corrosion without mechanical wear at the same elevated temperature, and (iii) a microstructurally modified variant with reduced phase boundary area.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies within the boundary conditions of elevated temperature (≈700 °C), corrosive media (chloride-containing sulfuric acid environment), mechanical sliding wear under specified loads, and for the specific eutectic microstructure of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy. It does not necessarily apply to different alloy systems or vastly different environmental conditions.
generation.uncertainty: There remains uncertainty in the quantitative separation of wear-induced oxide removal versus chemical breakdown of the oxide film, the exact kinetics of galvanic interactions at the microscopic level, and variability in oxide film formation across different regions of the microstructure. In addition, the extrapolation of controlled lab conditions to real-world service conditions may introduce scaling uncertainties.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a set of controlled sliding wear tests at 700 °C in a corrosive environment on three sets of samples: (a) the baseline AlCoCrFeNi2.1 with original lamellar spacing, (b) the same alloy with minimized phase boundary area achieved via thermo-mechanical processing (refined lamellar spacing), and (c) tests under isolated wear-only and corrosion-only conditions. Use in situ high-temperature SEM and electrochemical monitoring to track oxide formation/spallation and local corrosion activity at phase interfaces.
measurements: Quantitative rate of material loss (mass loss, wear track volume loss) for total degradation
Electrochemical corrosion current densities and pitting density measurements
High-resolution imaging and chemical mapping (e.g., EDS, XPS) of the oxide scale continuity at phase boundaries
Coefficient of friction (COF) measurements to correlate mechanical wear intensity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples with refined lamellar spacing do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in total degradation and localized galvanic corrosion at phase boundaries relative to the baseline, or if in situ observations do not reveal preferential oxide spallation at the softer fcc regions leading to localized corrosion, then the mechanistic hypothesis that the accelerated coupled degradation arises from wear-induced oxide film removal and subsequent galvanic action is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Next‐generation thermal barrier coating bond coats require not only exceptional oxidation resistance but also adequate mechanical properties. To evaluate this critical aspect, we compared the tensile performance of both alloys at room temperature. As shown in Figure S4, the commercial NiCoCrAlY alloy exhibits an ultimate tensile strength of 635 MPa with an elongation of 1.1%, while our MPEA demonstrates significantly superior properties with a strength of 711 MPa and an elongation of 2.7%. The simultaneous enhancement of both strength and ductility observed in our MPEA originates from its unique eutectic multi‐principal element alloy architecture, characterized by finely distributed and intimately alternating soft and hard phases—a structural advantage well documented in previous studies [, , ]. This mechanical superiority further highlights the potential of our MPEA as a high‐performance replacement for conventional NiCoCrAlY bond coats.

AbstractIn this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. Based on the above conclusions, the corrosion process of the EHEA in the test solution is schematically described in Figure 14. The passive films of few Al-Ni-rich phases are attacked by Cl− at lower temperature (Figure 14a2), and then occurs localized corrosion (Figure 14a3); while the passive films of Al-Ni-rich phases are damaged (Figure 14b2), and more Al-Ni-rich phases are dissolved at higher temperature (Figure 14b3). Metastable pits are preferentially created on the grain boundary or B2 phase. Pitting is enhanced by the effect of polarization. Due to autocatalysis by the caustic ions, the metastable pits gradually grow in the pitting corrosion area or the selective dissolution region. Moreover, the size of the selective dissolution region increases with temperature, and pitting occurs on the surface at various temperatures.

papers.title: A promising new class of high‐temperature alloys: eutectic high‐entropy alloys.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high‐entropy alloy featuring a lamellar microstructure with alternating soft (fcc) and hard (B2) phases
papers.approach: Designed via the eutectic concept; fabricated by casting and microstructurally characterized (XRD, SEM, DSC) to reveal uniform lamellar spacing and phase distribution
papers.findings: The alloy exhibited an excellent combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength maintained up to ~700 °C. The microstructure shows distinct compositional regions (Co, Cr, Fe rich vs. Al, Ni rich) that may influence local oxidation and corrosion behavior under degradation conditions.
papers.mechanism: The alternating phase structure is proposed to govern deformation and oxidation behavior; differential oxidation and potential galvanic interactions at phase boundaries can play a key role in coupled degradation.

papers.title: Corrosion Behavior of the AlCoCrFeNi₂.₁ Eutectic High‐Entropy Alloy in Chloride‐Containing Sulfuric Acid Solutions at Different Temperature
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high‐entropy alloy in acidic chloride environments
papers.approach: Electrochemical measurements, XPS, and SEM analysis at various temperatures to study passive film stability and pitting behavior
papers.findings: At low temperatures, a stable passive film forms; however, at elevated temperatures the passive film is damaged, leading to selective dissolution and pitting, especially at grain boundaries and among phase boundaries where Al-Ni–rich regions act anodically relative to Cr-enriched areas.
papers.mechanism: Proposes that the inherent chemical inhomogeneity (due to the eutectic microstructure) triggers localized galvanic corrosion; temperature exacerbates dissolution in certain phases, thereby coupling with mechanical damage from wear.

papers.title: High‐Temperature Wear Behaviour of Spark Plasma Sintered AlCoCrFeNiTi₀.₅ High‐Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 high‐entropy alloy produced via spark plasma sintering (SPS)
papers.approach: Reciprocating wear tests conducted over a range of elevated temperatures with phase analysis (XRD) and SEM of wear tracks
papers.findings: Wear resistance increases at elevated temperatures, attributed to the in situ formation and periodic regeneration of a protective oxide scale (spinel phase); COF trends correlate with oxide film wear and reformation cycles.
papers.mechanism: Suggests that a mechanically induced protective oxide layer forms dynamically under sliding, but under simultaneous corrosive attack, mechanical removal of this film can accelerate coupled degradation by exposing vulnerable phases.

papers.title: Outstanding 1200 °C Oxidation Resistance in a Novel Multi‐Principal Element Alloy via Lattice Distortion‐Induced Diffusion Suppression.
papers.system: Y and Hf co‐doped NiCoCrAl–type multi‐principal element alloy with a refined eutectic structure
papers.approach: High‐temperature oxidation tests at 1200 °C; comparison with conventional NiCoCrAlY; analysis of thermally grown oxide (TGO) and microstructural evolution
papers.findings: Exhibited a 59% lower TGO growth rate and negligible spallation after 500 h, with rapid initial formation of a protective Al₂O₃ scale; mechanical performance also superior at room temperature.
papers.mechanism: Lattice distortion induces diffusion suppression, while the refined eutectic microstructure favors early formation of protective oxide. These factors together delay degradation; however, under simultaneous wear and corrosion, mechanical removal of this stable oxide could be accelerated at vulnerable phase boundaries.

papers.title: Effect of Adding Molybdenum on Microstructure, Hardness, and Corrosion Resistance of an AlCoCrFeNiMo₀.₂₅ High‐Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNiMo0.25 high‐entropy alloy with modified phase chemistry
papers.approach: Comparative corrosion studies alongside microstructural and compositional analysis (EDS) following corrosion testing
papers.findings: Corrosion pits preferentially develop in Al and Ni rich regions (within grains or at boundaries) where galvanic coupling between Cr-rich (and Mo-influenced) areas and more active regions promotes localized degradation.
papers.mechanism: Attributes the accelerated degradation to galvanic corrosion stemming from phase segregation; differential element distribution results in micro-galvanic cells, which under wear conditions may further disrupt protective films.

established: Eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs) exhibit alternating soft and hard phases that contribute to balanced mechanical properties and influence oxidation/corrosion behavior.
Protective oxide films (e.g., Al2O3 or spinel phases) form at elevated temperatures and can enhance wear resistance under certain conditions.
Chemical inhomogeneity in multiphase HEAs leads to localized galvanic corrosion, especially at phase boundaries.
Lattice distortion effects, induced by alloying (e.g., Y, Hf, Mo), can suppress diffusion and improve oxidation resistance.

approaches_tried.approach: Designing eutectic microstructures to achieve alternating ductile and hard phases.
approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced mechanical strength and ductility maintained up to high temperatures; microstructural design influences oxidation and corrosion behavior.

approaches_tried.approach: Lattice distortion through specific alloying (e.g., Y/Hf co-doping) to suppress diffusion.
approaches_tried.outcome: Reduced TGO growth rate and improved oxidation resistance at ultra-high temperatures.

approaches_tried.approach: Spark plasma sintering to produce fine multiphase HEAs with enhanced oxide formation under wear.
approaches_tried.outcome: Improved wear resistance at elevated temperatures owing to dynamic protective oxide formation.

mechanisms: Lattice distortion‐induced diffusion suppression limits sustained oxidation.
Differential oxidation across eutectic phases leads to selective formation and breakdown of protective oxide films.
Galvanic corrosion emerging from chemical heterogeneity and phase boundary segregation.
Mechanical wear-induced removal of oxides, which accelerates exposure of vulnerable anodic phases.
disagreements: While some studies emphasize protective oxide layer formation as beneficial for wear resistance, others note that the same oxide film may be mechanically removed under synergistic wear–corrosion conditions, thereby accelerating degradation.
There is some divergence on the dominant site of degradation (grain interiors vs. grain/phase boundaries) with differing interpretations of the influence of element segregation.
open_questions: How do simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature interact at the microstructural level in multi-phase eutectic HEAs?
What is the quantitative contribution of mechanical oxide removal versus chemical film breakdown in the overall accelerated degradation process?
How does the interface between different eutectic phases evolve under combined cyclic mechanical and corrosive stresses?
opportunities: Develop controlled experiments comparing degradation under pure wear, pure corrosion, and simultaneous wear–corrosion conditions using identical eutectic HEA baselines.
Employ in situ high-temperature tribo-electrochemical testing to monitor the formation, degradation, and mechanical removal of oxide films at phase boundaries.
Explore combinatorial alloy design strategies that optimize eutectic phase distribution and incorporate diffusion-suppressing alloying additions to mitigate accelerated coupled degradation.
Implement advanced surface characterization techniques (e.g., in situ SEM, XPS) to specifically track galvanic interactions and oxide film spallation under simultaneous loading conditions.

directions.direction: Investigate the role of microstructural phase boundaries on degradation by comparing eutectic HEAs with different lamellar spacings.
directions.assessment: This approach directly targets the heterogeneity in phase chemistry and spacing that may drive localized galvanic interactions and mechanical spallation. Prior studies (e.g., PMC4145285::web::004::microstructure_and_phase_constitution) support the importance of alternating soft/hard phases, and the feasibility is high using standard casting and heat-treatment methods.

directions.direction: Examine the effect of alloying additions (e.g., Mo, Y, or Hf) that enhance lattice distortion and diffusion suppression, potentially stabilizing the protective oxide scale.
directions.assessment: Modifying the composition to enhance oxide scale stability could mitigate degradation; although the underlying physics of diffusion suppression is supported (PMC13067856::web::010::results), it may not address the mechanical removal due to wear directly.

directions.direction: Perform in situ high-temperature tribo-electrochemical tests to monitor the real-time formation and mechanical removal of protective oxide films at the phase boundaries.
directions.assessment: This study would directly capture wear–corrosion interactions and validate competing mechanisms such as oxide spallation. The technique is feasible using high-temperature cells and in situ SEM or electrochemical measurements; however, it requires complex instrumentation.

directions.direction: Use surface coatings or interfacial modifications (i.e. barrier layers) to decouple mechanical wear from galvanic corrosion at phase boundaries.
directions.assessment: While this approach can mitigate degradation, it simply masks the underlying degradation mechanism rather than explaining the fundamental cause. It may also conflict with the constraint of studying the intrinsic behavior of the base alloy.

directions.direction: Develop multi-scale computational models to simulate the coupled wear-corrosion process, incorporating mechanical removal of oxide films and localized electrochemical potential differences at phase interfaces.
directions.assessment: This direction can provide insights into the interplay between wear-induced film removal and localized galvanic corrosion. However, while supportive, simulations might need experimental validation to prove the single mechanistic hypothesis.

choice.direction: Investigate the role of microstructural phase boundaries on degradation by comparing eutectic HEAs with different lamellar spacings.
choice.why: This direction directly addresses the question of why degradation accelerates in a multiphase eutectic HEA under combined wear and corrosion at elevated temperature. Evidence suggests that heterogeneous phase boundaries are sites for preferential oxide formation and subsequent mechanical removal (PMC9319277::web::022::3_4_corrosion_observation, PMC7515071::web::012::3_2_wear_investigations). By controlling the microstructure (e.g. lamellar spacing) and thereby the extent of galvanic interactions, the experiment can yield clear differences that confirm or refute the mechanistic hypothesis.
